<reason>PRO built a coherent case (need, precedent, equity) and then found the decisive lever in CON's own opening: CON wants MRT licensed and privately available but not funded. PRO pressed this consistently—every safety risk CON raised (carryover, co-evolution, heritability, fifty-year horizon) applies identically to the privately conceived child, so CON's position collapses into a means test unless CON demands a ban. CON's licensing-vs-formulary analogy was a reasonable counter, but CON never gave a threshold when asked twice, leaving PRO's "permanent no dressed as delay" charge largely standing. PRO also neutralized the liability point cleanly: a reverted child imposes the same care costs the system would have borne anyway. CON's strongest late move—that public money buys "relatedness, a preference," not health—was live from its opening and is genuinely sharp, but PRO answered that it indicts the donor-egg IVF public systems already fund, and CON did not explain why the principle applies only here. CON's "narrower motion" objection also fell flat given the motion's own words. Both sides were grounded and disciplined; PRO made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [A2.1]–[A2.2] and its closing reprise [A5.1]–[A5.3]: seizing on CON's "private access under license" to show CON accepts the procedure's safety for paying families, turning the entire safety case into an equity problem CON never escaped despite the experimental-drug analogy.</best_rebuttal>
